newsitem.title: FINLAND: PARTEK CEO SEES GROWTH IN CONTAINERISATION.
newsitem.headline: PARTEK CEO SEES GROWTH IN CONTAINERISATION.

text.p: Growing volumes of containerised cargo worldwide will create growth opportunities for Finnish cargo handling equipment and building materials group Partek Oy Ab, its chief executive said on Thursday.

"World trade requires transport, and container handling is clearly outpacing growth in world trade," Partek president and CEO Christoffer Taxell told a news conference after the group had reported 1996 earnings down but above analysts' forecasts.
"This industrial solution is based on the fact that world trade is clearly growing faster than GDP," Taxell said.
He was referring to his group's strategy following a surprise merger unveiled last month with Finnish heavy vehicles maker Sisu Oy.

The strategy revolves around cooperation with Sisu in the engineering business via Partek's Cargotec unit, which fell to an operating loss of 25 milllion markka last year from a 151 million profit in 1995.
Partek group 1996 operating profit fell to 284 million markka from 380 million in 1995. More than half of the profit was generated by Partek's minerals unit, the company said.
The new Partek's six core businesses will be container handling machines, cargo handling equipment, forestry machines, tractors, minerals and insulation, Taxell said.
The link-up with Sisu gave Partek the volume to focus and grow, particularly in the cargo handling equipment business where the company has "a very strong market position," he said.
Based on 1996 performance, the new group has combined net sales of 12 billion markka against 6.2 billion for Partek alone.

Partek would look for "an independent solution" for its pre-cast concrete, Sisu trucks and real estate businesses, Taxell said, repeating earlier statements suggesting that it is ready to divest those units, but declining to elaborate.
A partial solution for Sisu trucks was found last month in a joint venture with French Renault's truck manufacturing division Renault V.I.
"We also are very confident that it is possible to seek growth and profitability in after-sales operations," Taxell added.
Even as the group redirects its focus towards the engineering business, its lucrative business operations are set to remain key components.
Taxell defined the merged group as: "A metal engineering company, which is a world leader in materials-handling, with two strong mineral-based businesses in the Baltic Sea region."

Immediate synergy benefits of the merger with Sisu would be worth about 100 million markka a year coming from savings in administration, legal structure, sourcing, improved capacity utilisation and information technology, Taxell said.

The dynamic benefits, the value of which Taxell did not estimate, would stem from such factors as geographical coverage of the sales network; cooperation in component making, spare parts and service; and sharing of best corporate practices.

"This strategy, which involves concentrating our strengths on certain core businesses ... (and) freeing up capital will give us the opportunity to focus and grow both by way of corporate acquisitions and organic growth," Taxell said.
